Australia and New Zealand require relevant foods to state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. That statement describes a short-term, dose-related gut effect rather than cumulative toxicity.

expanded_summary: Shellac is a natural resin secreted by lac insects on host trees. It is refined into a hard, glossy coating used on foods and many non-food products.
source_preparation_copy: Resinous lac material produced by insects is collected from branches, cleaned, melted or solvent-refined and formed into food-grade shellac.
fact_1_copy: Insect-derived resin rather than a plant wax.
fact_2_copy: Used as a glazing and protective coating.
fact_3_copy: Its insect origin can matter for vegan or personal ingredient choices.

tile_summary: Petrolatum, or petroleum jelly, is a highly refined semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons derived from petroleum.
expanded_summary: Petrolatum, or petroleum jelly, is a highly refined semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons derived from petroleum. Food-grade material is purified to much tighter specifications than crude petroleum products.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by refining and purifying selected petroleum fractions to remove unwanted components and create a stable semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture.
fact_1_copy: Used for surface coating, release or glazing functions in specified applications.

tile_summary: Oxidised polyethylene is a modified polyethylene wax.
expanded_summary: Oxidised polyethylene is a modified polyethylene wax. Controlled oxidation adds oxygen-containing groups to the polymer surface, changing its hardness and coating behaviour.
source_preparation_copy: Polyethylene is manufactured from ethylene and then deliberately oxidised under controlled conditions to produce the food-grade wax.
fact_1_copy: Used as a glazing or coating agent.
fact_2_copy: A synthetic polymer wax rather than a natural wax such as beeswax or carnauba.

tile_summary: L-cysteine hydrochloride is a salt of L-cysteine, a sulphur-containing amino acid found naturally in proteins.
expanded_summary: L-cysteine hydrochloride is a salt of L-cysteine, a sulphur-containing amino acid found naturally in proteins. In food processing it is particularly known for changing dough properties.
source_preparation_copy: Modern food-grade L-cysteine can be produced by microbial fermentation or other controlled manufacturing routes, then converted to the hydrochloride salt and purified.
fact_1_copy: Cysteine is a normal amino-acid component of many proteins.
fact_2_copy: Can act as a flour treatment agent by modifying disulphide bonds in dough proteins.
fact_3_copy: The additive number does not by itself disclose the manufacturing source, so source-specific dietary concerns require product or supplier information.

tile_summary: Nitrogen is an inert gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
expanded_summary: Nitrogen is an inert gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.

fact_1_copy: Used to displace oxygen, protect food from oxidation, create packaging atmospheres or provide pressure.
fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

expanded_summary: Nitrous oxide is a gas composed of nitrogen and oxygen, best known in food for pressurising and aerating whipped cream.
source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially from controlled decomposition of ammonium nitrate and highly purified.

fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

expanded_summary: Butane is a small hydrocarbon gas.

fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

expanded_summary: Isobutane is a branched isomer of butane.

fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

expanded_summary: Propane is a small hydrocarbon gas widely used as a fuel but also purified for specialised food-propellant use.

fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

tile_summary: Octafluorocyclobutane is a fully fluorinated cyclic gas.
expanded_summary: Octafluorocyclobutane is a fully fluorinated cyclic gas.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled fluorochemical synthesis and purified.
fact_1_copy: Used as a specialised propellant or packaging gas in limited applications.
fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

tile_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener.
expanded_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener. Its molecule contains a cyclic sulphamate structure and provides sweetness with very little mass compared with sugar.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by multi-step chemical synthesis and converted to the potassium salt.
fact_1_copy: Roughly 200 times sweeter than sucrose, depending on the food matrix.
fact_2_copy: Used to provide sweetness with little added energy and is often blended with other sweeteners.
fact_3_copy: Blending can reduce aftertaste and produce a sweetness profile closer to sugar.
evidence_copy: A 2025 European review concluded that intake of 950 was unlikely to be associated with cancer, disrupted glucose or insulin control, cardiovascular disease or organ toxicity. It set a daily safety limit of 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight and found that high-exposure estimates were generally below it. The review separately recommended a tighter limit for one manufacturing impurity, distinguishing product-purity control from the safety conclusion on the sweetener itself.
evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of acesulfame K E950 (2025)

tile_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose.
expanded_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose. It looks and behaves more like a bulk sugar ingredient than an ultra-intense sweetener.

fact_1_copy: Ordinary sucrose.
fact_2_copy: Less sweet than sucrose, so it contributes bulk as well as sweetness.
fact_3_copy: Common in sugar-free confectionery because it can provide structure, glassy texture and lower sweetness.

tile_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners.
expanded_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners. It is much sweeter than sugar and is used in very small amounts.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis; food products may use saccharin itself or approved soluble salts depending on the formulation.
fact_1_copy: Several hundred times sweeter than sucrose.
fact_2_copy: Used to provide intense sweetness with negligible bulk.
fact_3_copy: Saccharin has been used as a sweetener since the late 19th century.

tile_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms.
expanded_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms. The result is intensely sweet but metabolised very differently from ordinary sugar.
source_preparation_copy: Produced from sucrose through a controlled multi-step chlorination and purification process.
fact_1_copy: Sucrose — ordinary table sugar — is the structural starting point.
fact_2_copy: About 600 times sweeter than sucrose.
fact_3_copy: Used for intense sweetness and is relatively stable during many cooking and processing conditions.
evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority kept the daily safety limit for sucralose at 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight in 2026 and found estimated exposure from currently authorised uses below it in every population group. The same review could not support a proposed extension to more fine bakery products because the many possible baking times and temperatures left a question about forming chlorinated compounds. The reassuring conclusion covers current authorised uses; the unresolved issue concerns a proposed broader high-temperature use.
evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of sucralose E955 and proposed bakery extension (2026)

tile_summary: Alitame is a high-intensity sweetener built from amino-acid-derived components.
expanded_summary: Alitame is a high-intensity sweetener built from amino-acid-derived components. Its peptide-like structure is engineered for very strong sweetness.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled chemical synthesis from amino-acid-derived building blocks and purified.
fact_1_copy: Thousands of times sweeter than sucrose, so only very small amounts are needed.
fact_2_copy: Used as an intense sweetener rather than a bulk sugar replacement.

tile_summary: Thaumatin is an intensely sweet protein obtained from the West African katemfe fruit.
expanded_summary: Thaumatin is an intensely sweet protein obtained from the West African katemfe fruit. Unlike most high-intensity sweeteners, its sweetness comes from a protein rather than a small molecule.
source_preparation_copy: Extracted and purified from the arils of Thaumatococcus daniellii fruit.
fact_1_copy: Katemfe fruit from Thaumatococcus daniellii.
fact_2_copy: Extremely sweet by weight and also used to modify or enhance flavour.
fact_3_copy: It is a protein sweetener.

tile_summary: Steviol glycosides are intensely sweet compounds based on steviol, best known from the leaves of the stevia plant.
expanded_summary: Steviol glycosides are intensely sweet compounds based on steviol, best known from the leaves of the stevia plant. Modern food-grade preparations can contain different purified glycosides and may be made by extraction, enzymatic conversion or fermentation-based processes depending on the specification.
source_preparation_copy: Traditional preparations are extracted and purified from Stevia rebaudiana leaves; newer approved forms can use enzymes or microorganisms to convert or produce particular steviol glycosides.
fact_1_copy: Stevia leaves naturally contain several steviol glycosides, including stevioside and rebaudiosides.
fact_2_copy: Many individual steviol glycosides are hundreds of times sweeter than sucrose.
fact_3_label: Why the source label can be nuanced
fact_3_copy: The same additive family can include directly extracted and biotechnologically produced glycosides.

tile_summary: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.
expanded_summary: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemically modifying aspartame-related amino-acid components and purifying the resulting compound.
fact_1_copy: Several thousand times sweeter than sucrose.
fact_2_copy: Used at extremely low levels for intense sweetness.
fact_3_copy: Structurally related to aspartame but it is a distinct sweetener.

expanded_summary: Aspartame-acesulphame salt is a crystalline compound containing the two sweeteners aspartame and acesulphame in a fixed salt-like combination.
source_preparation_copy: Made by combining purified aspartame and acesulphame components under controlled conditions and crystallising the resulting compound.
fact_1_copy: Two established high-intensity sweetener components in one ingredient.
fact_2_copy: Provides a blended sweetness profile without adding the two sweeteners separately.
fact_3_copy: The ingredient contains aspartame-derived material as well as acesulphame.

tile_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups.
expanded_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups. They provide bulk and texture as well as sweetness.
source_preparation_copy: Starch is broken down to maltose/glucose-rich syrup and then hydrogenated; crystalline maltitol or mixed hydrogenated glucose syrup is purified for food use.
fact_1_copy: Usually starch-derived carbohydrate syrup.
fact_2_copy: Maltitol is less sweet than sucrose but much closer to sugar in bulk and texture than intense sweeteners are.
fact_3_copy: Widely used in sugar-reduced confectionery and fillings because it supplies body as well as sweetness.
evidence_copy: Maltitol is not fully absorbed, so larger servings can draw water into the bowel and be fermented, causing bloating or loose stools. A United Nations food-additive expert committee did not consider a numerical toxicological limit necessary for its assessed uses. Australia and New Zealand require relevant foods containing polyols to state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. Portion size and the combined amount of polyols matter more than one occurrence of 965 on a label.
evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: Warning and advisory statements (updated 2025-11-26)
evidence_source_2_link_label: United Nations food-additive expert committee: Maltitol INS 965 evaluation (1993)

tile_summary: Lactitol is a sugar alcohol made from lactose, the natural sugar in milk.
expanded_summary: Lactitol is a sugar alcohol made from lactose, the natural sugar in milk. Hydrogenation changes lactose into a less-sweet polyol used for bulk and texture.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by catalytic hydrogenation of lactose, followed by purification and crystallisation.
fact_1_copy: Lactose, the milk sugar.
fact_2_copy: Milder than sucrose.
fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener, texture ingredient and humectant.

tile_summary: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables.
expanded_summary: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables. It has sweetness close to sucrose and produces a noticeable cooling sensation in the mouth.
source_preparation_copy: Commercial xylitol is commonly made by hydrogenating xylose obtained from plant hemicellulose; fermentation routes also exist.
fact_1_copy: Industrial xylose can come from wood, corn cobs and other plant fibre streams.
fact_2_copy: Dissolving xylitol absorbs heat, creating the cooling effect familiar in sugar-free gum.
fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener, particularly in confectionery and oral-care-style foods.

tile_summary: Erythritol is a four-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and fermented foods.
expanded_summary: Erythritol is a four-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and fermented foods. Commercial erythritol is made mainly by fermentation of sugars.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting glucose with selected yeasts or fungi, then filtering, crystallising and purifying the erythritol.
fact_1_copy: Found naturally at low levels in some fruits, fermented foods and beverages.
fact_2_copy: About 60–80% as sweet as sucrose, with a cooling sensation.
fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener and texture ingredient.
evidence_copy: Higher blood erythritol levels have been associated with cardiovascular disease in observational studies. Europe's food-safety authority found that those blood levels do not necessarily measure erythritol eaten as an additive and concluded that the studies did not establish cause and effect. A better-established immediate effect is diarrhoea. The authority set an intake value of 0.5 grams per kilogram of body weight per day and estimated that some consumers could exceed it.
evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of erythritol E968 (2023)

tile_summary: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame.
expanded_summary: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame. A chemical modification dramatically increases its sweetness potency.

fact_1_copy: Tens of thousands of times sweeter than sucrose under some test conditions.
fact_2_copy: Used at extremely low levels for intense sweetness.
fact_3_copy: It is related to aspartame structurally but is a distinct molecule with different properties.

expanded_summary: Choline salts are forms of choline, an essential nutrient-like compound used by the body to make cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Different salt forms are used to make choline stable and practical in formulations.

fact_2_copy: Depending on the product, choline salts may serve nutritional or technological formulation purposes.
fact_3_copy: The additive entry can cover more than one choline salt form.

expanded_summary: Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars and dextrins. The enzyme family occurs naturally across plants, animals and microorganisms; food-grade preparations are commonly produced with selected microbes.
source_preparation_copy: Commercial food enzymes are usually produced by controlled fermentation with bacteria or fungi, followed by filtration and purification of the enzyme preparation.
fact_1_copy: Cuts alpha-1,4 bonds in starch, reducing viscosity and producing smaller carbohydrates.
fact_2_copy: Used in baking, brewing, starch processing and other applications where starch needs to be broken down.
fact_3_copy: An enzyme is a protein catalyst, not a conventional small-molecule additive.

fact_2_copy: Break proteins into smaller peptides and amino-acid fragments.
fact_3_copy: Used for tenderising, clarifying, modifying dough/protein texture and other processing purposes.

expanded_summary: Glucose oxidase is an enzyme that converts glucose and oxygen into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide. Food manufacturers use that reaction to remove oxygen or alter dough and preservation conditions.

fact_2_copy: Can strengthen dough, reduce oxygen in packaged systems or support preservation-related processing.

expanded_summary: Lipases are enzymes that break down fats by splitting fatty acids from glycerol. They occur widely in living organisms and food-grade preparations are commonly made with selected microorganisms.

expanded_summary: Polydextrose is a highly branched glucose polymer used as a low-sweetness bulking ingredient and soluble fibre-like material. It is designed to replace some of the bulk normally provided by sugar or fat.

source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes acetylation, followed by washing and purification.
fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

tile_summary: Triethyl citrate is the triethyl ester of citric acid.
expanded_summary: Triethyl citrate is the triethyl ester of citric acid. It is a clear, mildly oily liquid used as a solvent, carrier and plasticising ingredient in specialised food applications.
source_preparation_copy: Made by esterifying citric acid with ethanol and purifying the resulting triester.
fact_1_copy: Citric acid plus ethanol.
fact_2_copy: Used as a carrier/solvent, flavour-related processing ingredient or coating plasticiser depending on the application.

tile_summary: Triacetin is glycerol triacetate — a molecule made by attaching three acetic-acid-derived groups to glycerol.
expanded_summary: Triacetin is glycerol triacetate — a molecule made by attaching three acetic-acid-derived groups to glycerol. It is used mainly as a solvent, carrier and texture/plasticising ingredient.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying glycerol with acetic acid or acetic anhydride, then purified.
fact_1_copy: Glycerol plus acetate groups.
fact_2_copy: Used as a carrier for flavours, a humectant/solvent or a plasticiser in coatings and gum bases.

tile_summary: Propylene glycol is a small, colourless liquid that mixes readily with water and is useful for carrying flavours, colours and other ingredients.
expanded_summary: Propylene glycol is a small, colourless liquid that mixes readily with water and is useful for carrying flavours, colours and other ingredients. It also helps retain moisture.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by hydration of propylene oxide or related chemical routes, then highly purified for food use.
fact_1_copy: Used as a solvent/carrier, humectant and texture-related ingredient.
fact_2_copy: It is chemically different from ethylene glycol, the toxic compound associated with automotive antifreeze.

tile_summary: Polyethylene glycol 8000 is a high-molecular-weight water-soluble polymer made from repeating ethylene oxide units.
expanded_summary: Polyethylene glycol 8000 is a high-molecular-weight water-soluble polymer made from repeating ethylene oxide units. The '8000' refers to its approximate molecular-weight range, not an additive code.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled polymerisation of ethylene oxide and purified to a defined molecular-weight distribution.
fact_1_copy: A polyethylene glycol polymer, not polyethylene plastic.
fact_2_copy: Used in specialised coating, carrier or processing applications where its waxy, water-soluble properties are useful.

tile_summary: Calcium lignosulphonate is a water-soluble polymeric material derived from lignin, one of the structural components of wood.
expanded_summary: Calcium lignosulphonate is a water-soluble polymeric material derived from lignin, one of the structural components of wood. It is a refined by-product of sulphite wood pulping.
source_preparation_copy: Recovered from sulphite pulping liquor, purified, fractionated and converted to the calcium salt form.
fact_1_copy: Ultimately derived from wood lignin.
fact_2_copy: Used in limited applications as a carrier, binder or dispersing material.
fact_3_copy: It is not ground wood; it is a purified lignin-derived polymer fraction.

tile_summary: Quillaia extract type 1 is a less-purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria.
expanded_summary: Quillaia extract type 1 is a less-purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria. Its key components are saponins — plant molecules that can stabilise foam and emulsions.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by water extraction of soapbark tree material, followed by filtration and concentration; type 2 undergoes more extensive purification than type 1.
fact_1_copy: Quillaja saponaria, a South American tree also called soapbark.
fact_2_copy: Used as a foaming agent and emulsifier, especially in beverages.
fact_3_copy: The types differ mainly in purification and composition, not in the basic plant source.

consumer_display_name: Monk fruit extract or luo han guo extract
entry_title: Monk fruit extract or luo han guo extract
tile_summary: Monk fruit extract, or luo han guo extract, is an intensely sweet botanical extract from the fruit of Siraitia grosvenorii.
expanded_summary: Monk fruit extract, or luo han guo extract, is an intensely sweet botanical extract from the fruit of Siraitia grosvenorii. Its sweetness comes mainly from mogrosides such as mogroside V.
source_preparation_copy: The fruit is water-extracted; the sweet mogrosides are then filtered, concentrated and purified, often using adsorption/resin steps.
fact_1_copy: Monk fruit / luo han guo.
fact_2_copy: Mogrosides are intensely sweet, allowing small amounts of extract to replace some sugar sweetness.
fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.

tile_summary: Mushroom chitosan is a natural fungal cell-wall polymer sourced from Agaricus bisporus mushrooms.
expanded_summary: Mushroom chitosan is a natural fungal cell-wall polymer sourced from Agaricus bisporus mushrooms. Unlike conventional chitosan, which is often made from crustacean shells, this specified ingredient is mushroom-derived.
source_preparation_copy: Obtained from Agaricus bisporus fungal material and processed to isolate a chitosan/chitin-beta-glucan co-polymer preparation.
fact_1_copy: Mushroom rather than shellfish.
fact_2_copy: A natural co-polymer containing chitin/chitosan-related and beta-glucan components.
fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.

tile_summary: Sodium hydrosulphite, also called sodium dithionite, is a strong inorganic reducing agent.
expanded_summary: Sodium hydrosulphite, also called sodium dithionite, is a strong inorganic reducing agent. In food processing it is used for specialised bleaching or redox-control applications rather than as a general-purpose preservative.
source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled reduction of sulphur-containing inorganic compounds and crystallised as the sodium salt.
fact_1_copy: A powerful reducing agent — the chemical opposite of an oxidising agent.
fact_2_copy: Used only in specific processing applications where reduction or bleaching is required.
fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.

tile_summary: Sweet osmanthus ear glycolipids are natural glycolipid molecules made by the edible jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia during fermentation.
expanded_summary: Sweet osmanthus ear glycolipids are natural glycolipid molecules made by the edible jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia during fermentation. They act as preservatives against yeasts and moulds in certain beverages.
source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting glucose with a non-GM strain of Dacryopinax spathularia, then removing the fungal cells, purifying the glycolipids, pasteurising and spray-drying the product.
fact_1_copy: The producing organism is the edible sweet osmanthus ear / jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia.
fact_2_copy: Used as an antimicrobial preservative in specified beverages.
fact_3_copy: FSANZ currently lists this additive by name without a numeric Schedule 8 code.
